title: Best Permanent Basement Dehumidifier (2026): Installed Picks
dek: Retire the bucket for good: these installed, drain-connected units dry an entire basement and quietly keep it that way for years.
description: The best permanent basement dehumidifiers for 2026: installed, bucketless whole-basement units compared on capacity, drainage, ducting and warranty.
intro: A **permanent basement dehumidifier** is the point where you stop managing basement humidity and start ignoring it. Instead of a plastic portable you empty, move and replace every few summers, you get a heavy-duty unit that's mounted in place, plumbed to a drain and, if you like, ducted to the far corners of the space. It runs on a humidistat, drains on its own and is built to last a decade or more with basic filter care.

That's a different job from the portables in our [best dehumidifier for basement](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-basement/) guide, and from a [whole-house dehumidifier](/best/best-whole-house-dehumidifier/) that ties into your HVAC to dry every floor. Here we look at dedicated, installed units that treat the basement as its own zone, compared on rated capacity, coverage, drain and ducting options, low-temperature performance, efficiency and warranty.
topPicksLead: For most homes, the **Aprilaire E080** is the best permanent basement dehumidifier: it's ENERGY STAR Most Efficient, has capacity to spare for a typical basement and can run freestanding or feed short ducts.

products.whyWeLoveIt: The E080 is the sweet spot of Aprilaire's installed lineup: enough capacity for a large, damp lower level without the cost of the 100- and 130-pint models, plus a Most Efficient badge that pays off on a machine running every humid month for years.
products.performance: Aprilaire rates it at 80 pints a day under AHAM conditions and for spaces up to about 4,400 square feet, so a typical 1,000- to 2,000-square-foot basement sits well inside its comfort zone. Run it freestanding near the floor drain, or add short supply ducts to push dry air into a finished room it can't see. Compare it with its siblings in our [best Aprilaire dehumidifier](/best/best-aprilaire-dehumidifier/) guide.
products.notes: If the nearest drain is higher than the unit's outlet, budget for a condensate pump with a safety switch. Aprilaire's low-profile 4856 pump is made for the E-series.

Typical warranty on installed units, vs. 1–2 years for most portables
The humidity setpoint most basements should hold through the summer

blocks.text: One caution: installed units are rated under AHAM conditions (80°F, 60% humidity), while portables use the cooler 2019 DOE test. An 80-pint installed unit is not 30 pints ahead of a 50-pint portable — its lead is real, but smaller than the labels suggest.

sections.heading: How we pick permanent basement dehumidifiers

blocks.text: We don't run a test lab. We compare the information that's consistent across brands: AHAM capacity ratings, manufacturer coverage figures, ENERGY STAR listings, installation manuals (for drain, ducting, mounting and electrical requirements), warranty terms and the CPSC recall database.

For this guide we weighted how well a unit lives in a basement for years: continuous drainage, the lowest temperature it keeps working at, ducting and mounting options, filter access and warranty length. We then read owner reviews for recurring problems — pump failures, sensor drift, early compressor faults — and favored models where those reports are rare.

sections.heading: What to look for in a permanent basement dehumidifier

items.label: A drain plan before a model
items.text: Every pick here drains continuously — but only downhill unless you add a pump. Find your floor drain, sump pit or standpipe first, then choose the unit and spot.

items.label: Capacity rated the same way
items.text: Compare AHAM figures to AHAM figures. Ignore the bigger saturation number some brands print beside it.

items.label: Low-temperature operation
items.text: Unfinished basements can sit in the 50s °F in spring. Look for auto-defrost and a stated minimum operating temperature.

items.label: Ducting and mounting options
items.text: Ducts let one unit reach a finished room or a far corner; a hanging kit or platform keeps it off a floor that may get wet.
sub: Freestanding: easiest, recirculates the air around it
Ducted within the basement: pulls from one end, delivers to another
Hung from joists: frees floor space and keeps it above minor flooding

items.label: A remote or wall control
items.text: A wall-mounted control or app means you can check and change the setpoint without climbing behind the furnace. Set it using our [humidistat settings guide](/guides/dehumidifier-humidistat-settings-guide/).

items.label: Warranty and service access
items.text: Five to six years is normal. Check whether labor is covered and whether a pro install is required to keep it valid.

sections.heading: How to install a permanent dehumidifier in a basement

blocks.text: A freestanding install is well within reach for a handy homeowner. Tying into your HVAC ducts is a job for a licensed contractor.

items: **Pick the spot.** Near the drain, near an outlet, central to the space and with a couple of feet of clearance for filter changes. Keep it out of the path of a sump overflow.
**Get it off the floor.** Set it on a sturdy platform or hang it from the joists with the manufacturer's kit where the manual allows, so a small flood doesn't reach the electronics.
**Run the drain.** Route the condensate line with a steady downward slope to a floor drain, sump pit or standpipe. No uphill sections, sags or kinks.
**Add a pump if needed.** If the drain is higher than the outlet, install a condensate pump with an overflow safety switch wired to shut the dehumidifier off.
**Duct it (optional).** Pull return air from the dampest area and send supply air to the far end or to a finished room. Seal every joint with foil tape.
**Power it properly.** Plug it into a grounded outlet; a dedicated circuit avoids nuisance trips if it shares a circuit with a freezer or sump pump.
**Set and verify.** Start at 50%, then check with a separate hygrometer after a week and adjust toward 45% if the basement still smells musty.

blocks.title: Draining into a sump pit
blocks.text: It's one of the most common setups: the dehumidifier drains into the pit and the sump pump sends the water outside. Just make sure the line can't be pinched by the pit lid and that the sump pump is working — if it fails, the dehumidifier's water adds to the problem.

sections.heading: What does a permanent basement dehumidifier cost?

blocks.text: Installed-class units in the 70- to 130-pint range typically cost about $1,200 to $3,000; smaller 55-pint models cost less. A DIY freestanding install adds little beyond a platform, drain hose and perhaps a condensate pump. Contractor ducting, a new circuit or an HVAC tie-in is where costs climb — our [whole-house installation guide](/guides/whole-house-dehumidifier-installation/) has the numbers.

The payback comes from efficiency, a lifespan that can outlast several portables (see [how long dehumidifiers last](/guides/how-long-do-dehumidifiers-last/)) and the simple fact that a unit that drains itself never stops because nobody emptied the bucket.

For most basements, the **Aprilaire E080** is the permanent dehumidifier to buy: efficient, flexible to install and big enough for a damp lower level. Choose the **Santa Fe Compact70** when space next to the drain is tight, the **AlorAir HDi90** for the most capacity per dollar in a cool, unfinished basement, the **Aprilaire E100** for very large or wet spaces, and the **AlorAir HD55** for a smaller basement on a budget. Whatever you buy, plan the drain first and set the humidistat to 45–50%.

faqs.q: What is the best permanent basement dehumidifier?
faqs.a: For most homes, the Aprilaire E080. It's rated at 80 pints a day (AHAM), carries ENERGY STAR Most Efficient status, drains continuously and can be freestanding or ducted. The AlorAir Sentinel HDi90 is the value alternative, and the Santa Fe Compact70 fits tight utility rooms.

It's a heavy-duty unit designed to stay in one place for years: mounted on a platform or hung from joists, connected to a drain or condensate pump, and often ductable. Unlike a portable, it has no bucket to empty and typically carries a 5- to 6-year warranty.

faqs.q: Is a whole basement dehumidifier worth it?
faqs.a: If your basement needs dehumidifying most of the year, usually yes. You trade a higher upfront cost for no bucket duty, better efficiency per pint, a longer warranty and a unit that can last a decade or more. If the basement is only damp for a few weeks a year, a good portable is the better buy.

faqs.q: What size whole basement dehumidifier do I need?
faqs.a: For a typical 1,000- to 2,000-square-foot basement, a 70- to 80-pint (AHAM) installed unit is plenty in most climates. Go to 90–100 pints for very large basements, high water tables or condensation on the walls, and to 55 pints for small, moderately damp spaces.

faqs.q: Can a basement dehumidifier drain into a sump pump pit?
faqs.a: Yes, it's one of the most common setups. Run the line so it drops steadily into the pit and can't be pinched by the lid. If the sump is higher than the dehumidifier's outlet, add a condensate pump.

faqs.q: Can I install a permanent basement dehumidifier myself?
faqs.a: A freestanding install with a gravity drain is a reasonable DIY job. Tying the unit into HVAC ductwork, adding a new circuit or wiring controls to an air handler is best left to a licensed contractor, and some warranties require it.
